title: Expected value of a discrete random variable using SUMPRODUCT
scenario_markdown:
A regional automobile franchise models the daily vehicle sales volume $X$ at its flagship showroom using the following discrete probability mass function:

| Vehicles Sold ($x$) | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Probability $P(X = x)$** | $0.10$ | $0.25$ | $0.35$ | $0.20$ | $0.10$ |

Calculate the mathematical expectation (mean) $E[X]$, identify the standard spreadsheet formula, and interpret the resulting expected value in an operational planning context.
assumptions: X is a finite discrete random variable with support {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
Expected value is the probability-weighted sum of all possible outcomes
Spreadsheet implementation uses SUMPRODUCT across values and probabilities
source_refs: Course Module 2: Discrete Random Variables & Probability Distributions

approval.notes: Reviewed expectation calculation: E[X] = 0(0.10) + 1(0.25) + 2(0.35) + 3(0.20) + 4(0.10) = 1.95 cars/day. Confirmed Excel SUMPRODUCT implementation and long-run average interpretation.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is the expected number of vehicles sold per day, $E[X]$?

options.text_markdown: **$E[X] = 2.00\text{ vehicles}$**: The unweighted arithmetic average of the possible outcomes $\frac{0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4}{5} = 2.00$.
options.hint_markdown: A simple average assumes all outcomes are equally likely (each 0.20); expected value must weight each outcome by its actual probability.

options.text_markdown: **$E[X] = 2.00\text{ vehicles}$**: The outcome with the highest probability ($0.35$).
options.hint_markdown: The outcome with highest probability is the mode; expected value is the weighted average center of mass.

stages.explanation_markdown:
The expected value of a discrete random variable is the probability-weighted sum of all possible outcomes:

$$E[X] = \mu = \sum_{x} x \cdot P(X = x)$$
$$E[X] = 0(0.10) + 1(0.25) + 2(0.35) + 3(0.20) + 4(0.10)$$
$$E[X] = 0 + 0.25 + 0.70 + 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.95\text{ vehicles/day}$$

stages.prompt_markdown: Assuming outcomes $x$ are in cells `A2:A6` and probabilities $P(X=x)$ are in cells `B2:B6`, which Excel formula directly calculates $E[X]$?

options.text_markdown: **`=SUMPRODUCT(A2:A6, B2:B6)`**: Multiplies corresponding elements in both arrays and sums the products.
**`=AVERAGE(A2:A6)`**: Averages the values in column A.
options.hint_markdown: AVERAGE only calculates the unweighted mean of column A and completely ignores the probability weights in column B.

options.text_markdown: **`=PRODUCT(A2:A6, B2:B6)`**: Multiplies all ten numbers together.
options.hint_markdown: PRODUCT multiplies all numbers across both ranges together into a single scalar rather than performing paired multiplication and summation.

stages.explanation_markdown: In Microsoft Excel, `=SUMPRODUCT(array1, array2)` evaluates $\sum a_i b_i$ in a single formula call without requiring a helper column. Entering `=SUMPRODUCT(A2:A6, B2:B6)` yields exactly $1.95$.

stages.prompt_markdown: How should the dealership General Manager interpret the expected value $E[X] = 1.95$ vehicles?

options.text_markdown: **It is the theoretical long-run average daily sales over many operating days**: On any single day, the dealership can only sell an integer number of cars ($0, 1, 2, 3$, or $4$), but averaged over a month (e.g. 20 selling days), they can expect approximately $20 \times 1.95 = 39$ total cars.
Every day the dealership will sell almost exactly 2 cars, with fractional 0.05 carryover.
options.hint_markdown: Individual outcomes are discrete integers; expected value is a mathematical long-run summary mean that need not be a possible individual outcome.

options.text_markdown: The dealership is guaranteed to sell at least 1.95 vehicles each day.
options.hint_markdown: The minimum possible sale is 0 vehicles (which happens 10% of the time); expectation is not a lower bound.

stages.explanation_markdown: An expected value represents the **long-run center of mass** of the distribution over repeated independent realizations. Even though $1.95$ is not an integer in the support (you cannot sell $0.95$ of a car on any given Tuesday), over $100$ business days the dealership will sell approximately $195$ total vehicles.
